aṅga.notes: MN 116:6.10 names the privately awakened Buddha Aṅga. The country entry belongs only under aṅga 4. In DN 19 the quoted imināpaṅgena means ‘in this respect’. The country itself occurs at DN 19:36.8, where Campā is laid out for the Aṅgas. The packet misses the country lists in AN 3.70, 8.42, 8.43 and 8.45 because the English lists the countries one segment earlier. The Assapura setting is in MN 39 and MN 40, and the king’s allowance is in MN 94. The page matches to MN 38 and MN 95 are incidental.

aṅgulimāla.notes: Check the entry’s quotation of the act of truth. In MN 86:15.8 Aṅgulimāla begins ‘yatohaṁ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto’. The entry inserts ‘sabbaññutabuddhassa ariyassa’.

aṅguttarāpa.notes: MN 54 and MN 66 open at Āpaṇa in Aṅguttarāpa. The page matches also pick up MN 53 at Kapilavatthu and MN 65 at Sāvatthī.

aṅgīrasa.notes: DPD already has aṅgīrasa 1, ‘epithet of the Buddha’. The packet omits that sense, so the Buddha’s entry goes in others. Thag 10.1:10.2 also has the epithet in Aṅgīrasassappaṭimassa. Sujato puts the name in 10.1, one segment earlier, so the packet misses it. AN 5.194, SN 8.12 and SN 9.1 are incidental page matches.

aṭṭhaka.notes: MN 52 gives the householder Dasama’s origin in the compound aṭṭhakanāgaro. Neither candidate describes the town. The sage entry lists only eight of Aṭṭhaka’s nine companions. The suttas include Kassapa between Vāseṭṭha and Bhagu.

badarikārāma.notes: SN 22.89 places the sick Khemaka in the Jujube Tree Monastery. The adjacent SN 22.88 places the sick Assaji in a monastery at Rājagaha.

baka.notes: Baka’s claim that his world is permanent occurs in MN 49 and SN 6.4. The page match to SN 6.3 picks up the discourse about Brahmadeva.

bandhumatī.notes: DN 14:1.12.2 names Vipassī’s mother and 1.12.3 names the royal capital. A single choice for DN 14 would be wrong for one of those taps. Both entries cite DN i.7, which places them in DN 1 in error.

bhadda.notes: DN 16 and SN 55.10 include Bhadda among the deceased lay followers at Ñātika. The six SN dialogues identify Ānanda’s fellow monk. Thag 7.3 tells of Bhadda’s ordination at age seven. DPD groups him with the SN monk, but DPPN calls the identification tentative and the verse does not settle it. The feminine Bhaddā hits belong to other people. SN 45.15–17 and SN 47.20 are incidental page matches.

bhaddiya.notes: The two SN verses name Bhaddiya among the seven liberated in Avihā. AN 4.193 names the Licchavi, and AN 5.33 locates Jātiyā Wood at Bhaddiya. DPD calls this town Aṅga’s capital, while DN 19:36.8 and the Aṅga entry name Campā. AN 1.193–194 distinguish Kāḷīgodhā’s son from Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya. Neither monk has a candidate here. MN 68 gives only the monk’s name, and SN 55.48 calls its addressee a Sakyan. AN 4.200, SN 55.50, Thag 16.10 and Ud 7.10 contain chapter summaries. The page matches to SN 1.49, AN 5.32 and AN 4.192 are incidental.

bhaddā.notes: AN 5.50 identifies the deceased queen as King Muṇḍa’s wife. The packet has no sense for her. DN 21 names Timbaru’s daughter Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, and AN 1.243–244 distinguish the two nuns. The queen’s entry would misidentify all three. AN 5.49 concerns Pasenadi.

bhagu.notes: The entry describes the ancient hymn-maker. MN 68 and MN 128 mention a contemporary monk, and Thag 4.2 attributes verses to Bhagutthero. The packet’s Thag 4.12 hit is the chapter summary.

bhallika.notes: AN 1.248 explicitly calls the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika the first laymen to take refuge. Its Pali tapussabhallikā has a separate dictionary line. Thag 1.7 uses the variant Bhalliya given in the entry. AN 1.258–267 and 1.268–277 are incidental page matches.

bharata.notes: DN 19:36.6 spells the Sovīra capital Roruka, where the entry has Roruva. Thag 2.28 is attributed to the elder Bharata.

bhesakalāvana.notes: The Pali spells the name Bhesakaḷāvana. AN 4.55 and AN 8.30 explicitly place the Buddha in its deer park. AN 4.54 and AN 8.29 are incidental page matches.

bhuñjatī.notes: DN 21:1.10.1–2 calls her Bhūjati. Her attendance on the meditating Buddha and Sakka’s request identify her despite the packet’s zero mentions. The local forms resolve to the separate DPD lemma bhūjati. The sutta calls her Vessavaṇa’s paricārikā, his attendant. DPPN’s description of her as his wife goes beyond the wording here.
